title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 816–817 (Night 173, continuing nights-172), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 173 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān follows his vizier's counsel: he waits another year, and on a festival day of public audience, with emirs, viziers, lords of the realm and troops all assembled, he sends for his son and commands him before them all to marry, so that he may rejoice in him before he dies. The prince, seized by the folly of youth, refuses outright, even if he were made to drink the cups of death, and tells his father he is a man old in years and small in wits. Shamed before his court, the king has the mamluks seize and bind his son, and reviles him for answering so before his troops, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-third night,
sentences.n: The formula as before, with al-thālitha, “the third”, feminine to agree with layla.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ سَمِعَ كَلَامَ الْوَزِيرِ وَصَبَرَ سَنَةً أُخْرَى حَتَّى حَصَلَ يَوْمُ مَوْسِمٍ وَجَاءَ يَوْمُ حُكُومَةٍ وَتَكَامَلَ فِيهِ مَجْلِسُ الْمَلِكِ بِالْأُمَرَاءِ وَالْوُزَرَاءِ وَأَرْبَابِ الدَّوْلَةِ وَالْعَسَاكِرِ وَأَصْحَابِ الصَّوْلَةِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Shahramāna samiʿa kalāma al-wazīri wa-ṣabara sanatan ukhrā ḥattā ḥaṣala yawmu mawsimin wa-jāʾa yawmu ḥukūmatin wa-takāmala fīhi majlisu al-maliki bi-al-umarāʾi wa-al-wuzarāʾi wa-arbābi al-dawlati wa-al-ʿasākiri wa-aṣḥābi al-ṣawlati
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-king Shahramān heard (the) speech of the-vizier and waited a-year another, until came-about a-day of-festival and came a-day of-government, and became-complete in-it (the) assembly of the-king with-the-emirs and the-viziers and (the) lords of the-state (-awla) and the-troops and (the) holders of the-might (-awla).
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that King Shahramān heeded his vizier's words and waited one more year, until a festival day came round, a day of public audience, and the king's court was filled to the last place with emirs and viziers, the lords of the realm, the troops, and the men of power.
sentences.n: The print has بالامراو, a misprint for بالامراء, corrected here. Shahrazād again takes up the last words of the night before, now adding wa-ṣabara, “and waited”. yawm ḥukūma, “a day of government”, is the day of public audience the vizier advised. takāmala, Form VI, “to become complete”: the king's majlis, his assembly, filled until no one was missing, and bi- marks what filled it, “with the emirs …”. arbāb al-dawla, “the lords of the state”, are the great officers; aṣḥāb al-ṣawla, “the holders of might”, the men of force. The list closes on a rhyme, al-dawlati … al-ṣawlati, in the manner of sajʿ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَرْسَلَ خَلْفَ وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ قَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ أَبِيهِ ثَلٰثَ مَرَّاتٍ وَوَقَفَ مُكَتِّفًا يَدَيْهِ وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ قُدَّامَ أَبِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu arsala khalfa waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni fa-lammā ḥaḍara qabbala al-arḍa bayna yaday abīhi thalātha marrātin wa-waqafa mukattifan yadayhi warāʾa ẓahrihi quddāma abīhi
sentences.l: Then indeed-he sent behind his-son Qamar al-Zamān; and when he-came, he-kissed the-ground between (the) two-hands of his-father three times, and stood folding his-two-hands behind his-back in-front-of his-father.
sentences.i: Then he sent for his son Qamar al-Zamān, and when he came he kissed the ground before his father three times and stood before him with his hands clasped behind his back.
sentences.n: arsala khalfa, “to send after”, is to send for someone, as the vizier advised. bayna yaday, “between the two hands of”, means “before, in the presence of”. thalātha marrātin: with the feminine counted noun marra the numeral takes the form without -a; the print spells it ثلٰث, without the long alif, and marks it with the dagger alif. mukattifan, active participle of Form II kattafa, “to fold, clasp (the arms or hands)”, in the accusative as a ḥāl describing how he stood, and taking yadayhi as its object: a posture of respectful submission. The shadda of قبّل and of مكتّفا and the dagger alif of ثلٰث are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُوهُ اعْلَمْ يَا وَلَدِي أَنِّي مَا أَرْسَلْتُ إِلَيْكَ وَمَا أَحْضَرْتُكَ هَذِهِ الْمَرَّةَ قُدَّامَ هَذَا الْمَجْلِسِ وَجَمِيعُ أَهْلِ الدَّوْلَةِ حَاضِرُونَ بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا إِلَّا لِأَجْلِ أَنْ آمُرَكَ بِأَمْرٍ فَلَا تُخَالِفْنِي فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu abūhu iʿlam yā waladī annī mā arsaltu ilayka wa-mā aḥḍartuka hādhihi al-marrata quddāma hādhā al-majlisi wa-jamīʿu ahli al-dawlati ḥāḍirūna bayna aydīnā illā li-ajli an āmuraka bi-amrin fa-lā tukhālifnī fīhi
sentences.l: So said to-him his-father: Know, O my-son, that-I did not send to-you, and did not bring-you this the-time in-front-of this the-assembly, and all (the) people of the-state (are) present between our-hands, except for-the-sake that I-command-you with-a-matter; so do not oppose-me in-it.
sentences.i: His father said to him, “Know, my son, that I have sent for you and brought you here this time, before this assembly, with all the men of the realm present before us, for one purpose only: to give you a command. So do not go against me in it.
sentences.n: mā … illā, “not … except”, is the Arabic way of saying “only”: I sent for you for no reason but this. arsala ilā is to send a message to someone, here the same as arsala khalfa above. aḥḍara, Form IV, “to cause to be present, bring”. wa-jamīʿu ahli al-dawlati ḥāḍirūna is a nominal clause introduced by wa- describing the circumstances, “with all … present”. li-ajli an, “for the sake of (the fact) that”, with an and the subjunctive āmuraka. amara bi-, “to command someone (direct object) to do something (bi-)”: the verb chooses bi-, which marks the thing commanded. The print writes āmuraka with the madda, a precomposed آ. lā tukhālifnī, prohibitive: lā with the jussive of khālafa, Form III, “to oppose, disobey”. The shadda of الّا is printed.

sentences.t: وَذَلِكَ أَنْ تَتَزَوَّجَ لِأَنِّي أَشْتَهِي أَنْ أُزَوِّجَكَ بِابْنَةِ مَلِكٍ مِنَ الْمُلُوكِ وَأَفْرَحَ بِكَ قَبْلَ مَوْتِي
sentences.tr: wa-dhālika an tatazawwaja li-annī ashtahī an uzawwijaka bi-ibnati malikin mina al-mulūki wa-afraḥa bika qabla mawtī
sentences.l: And that (is) that you-marry, because-I desire that I-marry-you with (the) daughter of a-king from the-kings, and (that) I-rejoice in-you before my-death.
sentences.i: It is this: that you marry. For I long to marry you to the daughter of one of the kings, and to have joy of you before I die.”
sentences.n: wa-dhālika an …, “and that is that …”, spells out the command just announced. tatazawwaja, Form V of z-w-j, “to marry, take a wife”; uzawwijaka, Form II, “to marry (someone) off”: the person married off is the direct object and bi- marks the bride, “to the daughter of”. afraḥa is still governed by an, so it too is subjunctive; fariḥa bi- is “to rejoice in”, with bi- marking the one rejoiced in.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ أَبِيهِ ذَلِكَ أَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَي الْأَرْضِ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى أَبِيهِ وَقَدْ لَحِقَهُ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ جُنُونُ الصِّبَا وَجَهْلُ الشَّبِيبَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni min abīhi dhālika aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi sāʿatan thumma rafaʿa raʾsahu ilā abīhi wa-qad laḥiqahu fī tilka al-sāʿati junūnu al-ṣibā wa-jahlu al-shabībati
sentences.l: And when heard Qamar al-Zamān from his-father that, he-bowed with-his-head to the-ground an-hour; then he-raised his-head to his-father, and (there) had overtaken-him in that hour (the) madness of the-boyhood and (the) ignorance of the-youth.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān heard this from his father, he bowed his head to the ground for a while; then he raised his head to his father, for in that hour the madness of boyhood and the folly of youth had come over him,
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV, “to lower the eyes, bow the head in silence”; the head may be its object or, as here, follow bi-, “with his head”. The print spells the first ilā الي, with a dotted ي, and the second الى; both are ilā. sāʿatan is an accusative of duration, “for an hour”, i.e. a while. wa-qad laḥiqahu is a circumstantial clause: qad with the perfect gives a past already accomplished, “madness had overtaken him”. junūn al-ṣibā wa-jahl al-shabība, “the madness of boyhood and the folly of youth”, is a pair of near-synonyms, a favourite pattern of the narrator's. The print spells raʾs with the hamza on the alif, a precomposed أ.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ أَمَّا أَنَا فَلَا أَتَزَوَّجُ أَبَدًا وَلَوْ سُقِيتُ كُؤُسَ الرَّدَى وَأَمَّا أَنْتَ فَرَجُلٌ كَبِيرُ السِّنِّ صَغِيرُ الْعَقْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu ammā anā fa-lā atazawwaju abadan wa-law suqītu kuʾusa al-radā wa-ammā anta fa-rajulun kabīru al-sinni ṣaghīru al-ʿaqli
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: As-for I, then not I-marry ever, even if I-were-made-to-drink (the) cups of the-death; and as-for you, then (you are) a-man great of the-age, small of the-mind.
sentences.i: and he said to him, “As for me, I will never marry, even if I were made to drink the cups of death. And as for you, you are a man old in years and small in wits.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for …, (then)”: the fa- regularly opens what is said about the topic, and the two halves balance, ammā anā … wa-ammā anta. lā with the imperfect atazawwaju makes a flat refusal, “I do not, will not marry”. wa-law, “even if”; suqītu is the passive of saqā, “to give to drink”, with kuʾūs as its second object. kuʾūs is the plural of kaʾs, “cup”; the print writes it كؤس, with the hamza seat printed and the long vowel's waw left out, and it is read here as printed, kuʾus (Classical kuʾūs). kaʾs al-radā, “the cup of death”, is a stock phrase. kabīru al-sinni ṣaghīru al-ʿaqli, “great of age, small of mind”: each adjective stands in construct with the thing in which it holds, and the two are set against each other. The shadda of السنّ is printed.

sentences.t: أَلَيْسَ أَنَّكَ سَأَلْتَنِي قَبْلَ هَذَا الْيَوْمِ مَرَّتَيْنِ غَيْرَ هَذِهِ الْمَرَّةِ فِي شَانِ الزَّوَاجِ وَأَنَا لَا أُجِيبُكَ إِلَى ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: a-laysa annaka saʾaltanī qabla hādhā al-yawmi marratayni ghayra hādhihi al-marrati fī shāni al-zawāji wa-anā lā ujībuka ilā dhālika
sentences.l: Is-it-not that-you asked-me before this the-day two-times other-than this the-time in (the) matter of the-marriage, and I not I-grant-you to that?
sentences.i: Did you not ask me twice before today, besides this time, about marriage, and I would not consent to it?”
sentences.n: a-laysa, “is it not?”, the interrogative a- on laysa; laysa followed by an anna-clause, “is it not (the case) that you …”, is a loose, spoken construction, where Classical usage would simply say a-lam tasʾalnī. The print writes the hamza of saʾaltanī on the alif, a precomposed أ. marratayni, dual of marra, an adverbial accusative, “twice”; ghayra hādhihi al-marrati, “other than this time”. fī shāni, “in the matter of”: the print writes shaʾn without its hamza, شان, and it is read shān, as in spoken Arabic. wa-anā lā ujībuka is a circumstantial clause: the imperfect describes a refusal that held each time, “while I would not grant you”. ajāba ilā, Form IV, “to grant someone (direct object) something (ilā)”: ilā marks what is asked for. The shadda of مرّتين is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ فَكَّ كِتَافَ يَدَيْهِ وَشَمَّرَ عَنْ ذِرَاعَيْهِ قُدَّامَ أَبِيهِ وَهُوَ فِي غَيْظِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni fakka kitāfa yadayhi wa-shammara ʿan dhirāʿayhi quddāma abīhi wa-huwa fī ghayẓihi
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān undid (the) folding of his-two-hands and bared (from) his-two-forearms before his-father, and he (was) in his-rage,
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān unclasped his hands and rolled back his sleeves from his forearms in front of his father, in the heat of his anger;
sentences.n: kitāf is properly the cord that ties a man's arms behind him, and kattafa yadayhi is “to pinion his hands”; but the same verb is used of folding the hands or arms across the body, the posture of a servant standing before his lord. The prince has stood so before his father, and now fakka, “undid”, that respectful clasp. shammara ʿan dhirāʿayhi, Form II, “to tuck up (the sleeve) from the forearms”, is the gesture of a man making ready to fight or to set to work: ʿan marks what is laid bare. quddāma, “in front of”, as before; the lexicons record it beside amāma. wa-huwa fī ghayẓihi, “and he in his rage”, is a circumstantial clause with wa-. The shaddas of فكّ, شمّر are printed.

sentences.t: وَتَكَلَّمَ مَعَ أَبِيهِ بِكَلَامٍ كَثِيرٍ وَانْزَعَجَ خَاطِرُهُ فَخَجِلَ أَبُوهُ وَاسْتَحَى لِأَنَّهُ حَصَلَ ذَلِكَ قُدَّامَ أَرْبَابِ دَوْلَتِهِ وَالْعَسَاكِرِ الْحَاضِرِينَ فِى الْمَوْسِمِ
sentences.tr: wa-takallama maʿa abīhi bi-kalāmin kathīrin wa-inzaʿaja khāṭiruhu fa-khajila abūhu wa-istaḥā li-annahu ḥaṣala dhālika quddāma arbābi dawlatihi wa-al-ʿasākiri al-ḥāḍirīna fī al-mawsimi
sentences.l: and he-spoke with his-father with many words, and was-agitated his-mind; so was-abashed his-father and was-ashamed, because-it came-about, that, before (the) lords of his-state and the-troops the-present-ones at the-festival.
sentences.i: he said a great deal to his father and his temper was roused. His father was abashed and ashamed, for this had happened before the grandees of his realm and the troops gathered for the festival.
sentences.n: takallama maʿa, Form V, “to speak with”; bi-kalāmin kathīrin, “with much speech”: bi- marks the words he used. inzaʿaja, Form VII, “to be disturbed, upset”; khāṭir, “mind, mood”, is its subject. istaḥā, “to be ashamed”, is the shortened form of Classical istaḥyā (Form X of ḥ-y-y), which the lexicons also record. li-annahu ḥaṣala dhālika, “because it came about, that thing”: li- gives the cause, and -hu is the pronoun of the matter, anticipating the clause. arbāb dawlatihi, “the lords of his state”, are the officers of the realm. The print writes fī here with ى, a few words after writing it with ي.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ لَحِقَتْهُ شَهَامَةُ الْمُلْكِ فَصَرَخَ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ فَأَرْعَبَهُ وَصَرَخَ عَلَى الْمَمَالِيكِ الَّذِينَ قُدَّامَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُمْ أَمْسِكُوهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika Shahramāna laḥiqathu shahāmatu al-mulki fa-ṣarakha ʿalā waladihi fa-arʿabahu wa-ṣarakha ʿalā al-mamālīki alladhīna quddāmahu wa-qāla lahum amsikūhu
sentences.l: Then indeed the-king Shahramān, overtook-him (the) high-spirit of the-kingship, so he-shouted at his-son and terrified-him, and he-shouted at the-mamluks who (were) before-him and said to-them: Seize-him!
sentences.i: Then the pride of kingship rose up in King Shahramān. He shouted at his son and struck terror into him, and he shouted to the mamluks standing before him, “Seize him!”
sentences.n: al-malika Shahramāna is put first, after thumma inna, and picked up by -hu in laḥiqathu, “(it) overtook him”; the verb is feminine to agree with shahāma, “high spirit, proud resolve”. shahāmatu al-mulki is read “the pride of kingship”; the same letters could be shahāmatu al-maliki, “the king's pride”, with little difference. ṣarakha ʿalā, “to shout at”: ʿalā marks the one shouted at. arʿaba, Form IV, “to frighten, terrify”. amsikūhu, Form IV imperative plural, “seize him”; the next sentence uses Form I masakūhu for the same act. The shadda of قدّامه is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَسَابَقَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْمَمَالِيكُ فَمَسَكُوهُ وَأَحْضَرُوهُ قُدَّامَهُ فَأَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يُكَتِّفُوهُ فَكَتَّفُوهُ وَقَدَّمُوهُ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-tasābaqat ilayhi al-mamālīku fa-masakūhu wa-aḥḍarūhu quddāmahu fa-amarahum an yukattifūhu fa-kattafūhu wa-qaddamūhu bayna yadayi al-maliki
sentences.l: So raced-one-another to-him the-mamluks, and they-seized-him and brought-him before-him; and he-ordered-them that they-pinion-him, so they-pinioned-him and set-him-forward between (the) two-hands of the-king,
sentences.i: The mamluks rushed at him, each trying to be first. They seized him and brought him before the king, who ordered them to bind his arms. So they bound him and set him before the king,
sentences.n: tasābaqa, Form VI, “to race one another”: the feminine singular verb agrees with the broken plural al-mamālīku, which follows it. masakūhu, “they seized him”, from Form I masaka. The lexicons know masaka beside the commoner Form IV amsaka, but with a direct object it is the everyday later usage; the text has both in two lines. aḥḍara, Form IV, “to bring”. kattafa, Form II, “to tie someone's arms behind him”; an yukattifūhu is subjunctive after an, and the nūn of the plural is dropped. The hands the prince had just unclasped are now tied. qaddama, Form II, “to bring forward, present”. bayna yaday, “between the two hands of”, means “in the presence of”; the print writes the dual with ى. The shadda of يكتّفوه is printed.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ مُطْرِقٌ رَأْسَهُ مِنَ الْخَوْفِ وَالْوَجَلِ وَتَكَلَّلَ جَبِينُهُ وَوَجْهُهُ بِالْعَرَقِ وَاشْتَدَّ بِهِ الْحَيَاءُ وَالْخَجَلُ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa muṭriqun raʾsahu mina al-khawfi wa-al-wajali wa-takallala jabīnuhu wa-wajhuhu bi-al-ʿaraqi wa-ishtadda bihi al-ḥayāʾu wa-al-khajalu
sentences.l: and he (was) lowering his-head from the-fear and the-dread (-al), and beaded his-brow and his-face with the-sweat, and grew-strong upon-him the-shame and the-abashment (-al).
sentences.i: and he stood with his head bowed in fear and dread, his brow and face beaded with sweat, overcome with shame and confusion.
sentences.n: A circumstantial clause, wa-huwa muṭriqun, “he bowing”: muṭriq is the active participle of Form IV aṭraqa, “to lower (the head), look down”, and like its verb it takes raʾsahu as its object. min gives the cause, “out of fear”. The pairs al-khawfi wa-al-wajali and al-ḥayāʾu wa-al-khajalu rhyme. takallala, Form V of k-l-l, “to be crowned, wreathed”: the sweat stands on his brow like a circlet of pearls; bi- marks what crowns it. ishtadda bihi, Form VIII, “(it) grew hard upon him”: bi- marks the one it bears down on. The hamza of رأسه and the shaddas of تكلّل and اشتدّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ شَتَمَهُ أَبُوهُ وَسَبَّهُ وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ يَاوَلَدَ الزِّنَا وَتَرْبِيَةَ الْخَنَا كَيْفَ يَكُونُ هَذَا جَوَابَكَ لِي بَيْنَ عَسَاكِرِي وَجُيُوشِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika shatamahu abūhu wa-sabbahu wa-qāla lahu waylaka yā walada al-zinā wa-tarbiyata al-khanā kayfa yakūnu hādhā jawābaka lī bayna ʿasākirī wa-juyūshī
sentences.l: So at that, reviled-him his-father and cursed-him, and said to-him: Woe-to-you, O son of the-fornication (-nā) and nursling of the-obscenity (-nā)! How is this your-answer to-me among my-troops and my-armies?
sentences.i: At that his father reviled him and cursed him, and said, “Woe to you, you bastard, you nursling of filth! How can this be your answer to me, in front of my troops and my armies?
sentences.n: shatama and sabba, “to revile” and “to abuse, curse”, are near synonyms paired for force. waylaka, “woe to you”: wayl is put in the accusative with the pronoun. walada al-zinā, “son of fornication”, is the common insult “bastard”, and tarbiyata al-khanā, “rearing of obscenity”, one brought up in filth; the two rhyme (al-zinā / al-khanā), walada is accusative as a vocative in construct after yā, and tarbiyata follows it in the same case. The insult strikes back at the speaker's own house, as such curses do, but it is meant only as abuse. The print runs yā into walada as one word, as it often does. In kayfa yakūnu hādhā jawābaka, hādhā is the subject of yakūnu and jawābaka its predicate, accusative. The shadda of سبّه is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ أَنْتَ إِلَى الْآنَ مَا أَدَّبَكَ أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin anta ilā al-āna mā addabaka aḥadun
sentences.l: But you, until the-now, not has-disciplined-you anyone.
sentences.i: But no one has taught you manners to this day.
sentences.n: The print has احدوا درك, a misprint for احد وادرك (the space misplaced), corrected here. wa-lākin anta, “but you”: lākin, the light form, is followed by a whole clause: anta is put first as its topic and picked up by -ka in addabaka. addaba, Form II of ʾ-d-b, “to train in good manners, discipline, chastise”; mā with the perfect negates it, “no one has disciplined you”. The madda of الآن and the shadda of ادّبك are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The print has درك, joined in error to the previous word; see the note before. The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning. The formula rhymes al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi.
